summary: The only plug-in Defender is the 110 P300e, a 221kW 2.0-litre petrol hybrid sold in two trims and no other body length. Reviewers agree it keeps everything that makes a Defender a Defender — the twin-speed transfer case, the air suspension, the 3000kg tow rating — and adds around 48km of quiet electric running that suits a Melbourne commute. Where they split is whether that is worth the money: the battery costs boot space, a third-row seat and roughly $13,500-$17,500 over the equivalent D350 diesel, and the fuel saving only materialises if the car is plugged in nightly.
pros: The only Defender you can plug in: about 48km of WLTP electric range covers a typical Melbourne commute, and it is one of the few PHEVs at any price with DC fast charging rather than AC only (Land Rover quotes 0-80 per cent in about 30 minutes at up to 40kW; CarExpert's Australian data lists 32kW).

Keeps the Defender's touring hardware intact — 3000kg braked towing, a 90-litre tank, twin-speed transfer case and up to 900mm wading on air suspension — so the battery is added capability rather than a substitution.

Clears both Australian tax tests: 78g/km CO2 on the Australian label is well inside Victoria's 120g/km green-car duty threshold, and the 3.1L/100km combined label sits under the 3.5L/100km fuel-efficient LCT limit that lifts the threshold from $80,809 to $91,661.

Five-year, unlimited-kilometre warranty with five years of roadside assistance and six-year anti-corrosion cover, level with Volvo and BMW rather than the shorter terms Land Rover Australia used to offer.
cons: CarExpert measured 9.7L/100km on the same drivetrain once the battery was flat and never recharged, against a 3.1L/100km label, so a buyer without home charging is running a 2.5-tonne car on a small four-cylinder engine and paying for it in fuel.
The pack eats the boot: the P300e has 696 litres behind the second row and 1759 litres folded against 786 and 1875 litres for a non-hybrid 110, with the loadspace floor raised 36mm over the battery.
No third row. Land Rover does not offer the seven-seat Family Pack on the P300e, so a family that needs six or seven seats has to take a D350 110 or step up to a 130.
Braked towing falls to 3000kg against 3500kg for the D350 and P425, and the PHEV carries roughly 100kg more kerb weight, so it is the worst Defender in the range for a heavy trailer.

At $136,800 and $149,000 before on-road costs after the MY27 price rise, it asks $17,500 and $13,500 more than the D350 X-Dynamic SE and HSE, and it is well past the $75,000 cap in the 2027 FBT phase-down as well as both LCT thresholds.
